never allow myself to feel or express anger
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette:
Ethan, a 27-year-old journalist of South Eastern Asian descent, had always been passionate about uncovering the truth, but the truth of his own life had become too painful to confront. Just a year ago, he had endured a harrowing experience - physical abuse at the hands of his romantic partner. The memories of that night were etched into his mind, vividly replaying in a loop that felt more like an intrusion than a recollection. Each time he thought about it, the visceral sensations returned, making him feel as if he were reliving the trauma all over again. The physical pain he had felt during the assault resurfaced, a relentless reminder that the event was not confined to the past. 

In the aftermath of that night, Ethan's world had begun to shrink. He found himself avoiding public transport, particularly buses, where the crowded conditions felt suffocating and overwhelming. Each time he was confronted with the chaos of a bus, the memory of the attack would surface, leaving him anxious and desperate to escape. In those moments, Ethan would often turn to self-blame, telling himself that he must have done something to provoke the situation, which only reinforced his desire to avoid these crowded spaces altogether. Each time he found himself in a crowded bus, the anxiety would bubble up, leading him to self-blame once again, and he would quickly seek to escape the situation, reinforcing his pattern of avoidance. To avoid that intense discomfort, he began to seek out alternative routes, even if it meant longer commutes. Memories of the abuse would flash before him, leaving him feeling exposed and vulnerable, as if he were still trapped in that moment. The mere presence of men in his vicinity triggered a surge of anxiety, causing him to withdraw and isolate himself. These moments of heightened anxiety often led Ethan to engage in self-blame, convincing himself that he must have done something to provoke it, which only reinforced his sense of inadequacy. He had come to believe that anyone could be a threat, and this mistrust seeped into his daily life, making it impossible for him to feel safe even in familiar settings. The more he avoided these situations, the more inadequate and helpless he felt - a feeling that only reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of safety or love.

Ethan's coping strategies became a shadow of his former self. The memories of the abuse would often flood back during moments of vulnerability, and to manage the overwhelming feelings, he would engage in self-blame, convincing himself that he was somehow responsible for what had happened. Each time he indulged in this self-blame, he felt an increasing sense of inadequacy, further entrenching the belief that he was fragile and incapable of handling the trauma, which only deepened his negative self-perception. The reliance on these maladaptive strategies brought with it a troubling realization that he was not only fragile but also dependent on these behaviors to cope, reinforcing the belief that he could not handle his trauma alone. The ongoing reliance on these maladaptive strategies reinforced his belief that he was weaker than others, or else he would have been able to cope without resorting to them. He often engaged in a pattern of self-blame, ruminating over what he might have done differently to prevent the violence. Each time he resorted to these maladaptive strategies, it reinforced his belief that he was fragile, unable to cope without hiding his true feelings, adding to his sense of being unworthy of love and safety. These thoughts spiraled into darker places, feeding his belief that he was somehow responsible for the abuse. He would suppress his anger, convinced that expressing it would only lead to further harm, both to himself and to those around him. Each time he engaged in these maladaptive strategies, it reinforced the belief that he was fragile, that he couldn't cope without hiding his true feelings, further entrenching his negative self-image. This emotional suppression manifested in other ways, including a troubling relationship with food; he found himself undereating as a way to cope, convinced that by restricting his intake, he could regain some semblance of control over his life.

As days turned into months, Ethan's sense of safety deteriorated further. He would wake in the middle of the night, gripped by fear, convinced that danger lurked just beyond his door. When he heard the clock tick longer than expected or when a simple delay occurred, his mind would race to dark possibilities, convinced that something bad was about to happen. This heightened sense of threat was compounded by his negative appraisals of the world around him. Feeling this constant sense of danger quietly confirmed the thought he worked hard to resist - that he was simply not the kind of person who got to feel safe. The constant awareness of potential danger convinced him that he was not the kind of person who deserved safety or peace, further entrenching his negative self-image. This belief intensified his reactions to even minor triggers, such as a loud noise or a sudden movement, as he became convinced that they were further proof of the world's inherent danger. Once he had internalized this belief, even minor incidents like a loud noise or a sudden movement would trigger a wave of anxiety, confirming his fears that the world was unsafe and that he was perpetually at risk. Feeling constantly on edge, he had come to accept that this fear was a reflection of his own inadequacy, a belief that he was not the kind of person who deserved to feel safe. This pervasive sense of threat confirmed the thought he worked hard to resist - that he was simply not meant to experience peace in his life. This pervasive sense of threat clouded his judgment, making him believe that even the most mundane situations could lead to danger, thus confirming his negative views of himself and the world. The constant sense of danger validated his most fearful thoughts, leading him to conclude that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, which made the world feel even more hostile. He felt a deep-seated conviction that people, in general, could not be trusted, which only fueled his anxiety and avoidance of social interactions. This belief that everyone around him could pose a threat made him hyper-vigilant, believing that he was always in danger, which in turn reinforced his sense of isolation and mistrust. He became increasingly convinced that the world was a dangerous place where harm was always just around the corner.

The memories of the abuse served as a catalyst for his negative beliefs, reinforcing a cycle of self-doubt and mistrust. Every time he recalled the event, the emotional overwhelm would wash over him, leaving him breathless and paralyzed, unable to engage with the reality of his surroundings. After such memories surfaced, he often found himself thinking that if this kept happening, there must be something deeply wrong with him, reinforcing the negative beliefs he had developed about his own worth. This cycle perpetuated a negative appraisal of himself, making him believe that he was inherently flawed and unworthy of safety, further entrenching his feelings of inadequacy. Each time the trauma replayed in his mind, it deepened his conviction that he had somehow failed to protect himself, leading him to internalize a harmful narrative about his inadequacy. These vivid memories led him to internalize a negative self-perception, convincing him that he had somehow let this happen and that it indicated something fundamentally wrong with him. Each time the trauma replayed in his mind, it deepened his belief that he was somehow responsible for the violence, leading him to think of himself as a target rather than a victim. These memories were not distant echoes; they felt immediate and raw, leading him to believe he could never truly escape the impact of the trauma. Each recollection further intensified his belief that he was inadequate, unworthy of love, and unfit to trust anyone.

Now, as Ethan sits in a therapist's office for the first time, he feels a flicker of hope amidst the overwhelming shadows of his past. He is terrified that he will never be able to reclaim his sense of safety or self-worth, yet he longs to break free from the chains of his memories and the fear that has come to dominate his life. He knows he cannot continue to live in isolation, paralyzed by anxiety and mistrust. The journey ahead feels daunting, but the desire to regain control over his life is stronger than the fear that has held him captive for so long.

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Ethan, a 27-year-old journalist of South Eastern Asian descent, had always been passionate about uncovering the truth, but the truth of his own life had become too painful to confront. Just a year ago, he had endured a harrowing experience — physical abuse at the hands of his romantic partner. The memories of that night were etched into his mind, vividly replaying in a loop that felt more like an intrusion than a recollection. Each time he thought about it, the visceral sensations returned, making him feel as if he were reliving the trauma all over again. The physical pain he had felt during the assault resurfaced, a relentless reminder that the event was not confined to the past. 

In the aftermath of that night, Ethan's world had begun to shrink. He found himself avoiding public transport, particularly buses, where the crowded conditions felt suffocating and overwhelming. Each time he was confronted with the chaos of a bus, the memory of the attack would surface, leaving him anxious and desperate to escape. To avoid that intense discomfort, he began to seek out alternative routes, even if it meant longer commutes. Memories of the abuse would flash before him, leaving him feeling exposed and vulnerable, as if he were still trapped in that moment. The mere presence of men in his vicinity triggered a surge of anxiety, causing him to withdraw and isolate himself. These moments of heightened anxiety often led Ethan to engage in self-blame, convincing himself that he must have done something to provoke it, which only reinforced his sense of inadequacy. He had come to believe that anyone could be a threat, and this mistrust seeped into his daily life, making it impossible for him to feel safe even in familiar settings. The more he avoided these situations, the more inadequate and helpless he felt — a feeling that only reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of safety or love.

Ethan's coping strategies became a shadow of his former self. The memories of the abuse would often flood back during moments of vulnerability, and to manage the overwhelming feelings, he would engage in self-blame, convincing himself that he was somehow responsible for what had happened. Each time he indulged in this self-blame, he felt an increasing sense of inadequacy, further entrenching the belief that he was fragile and incapable of handling the trauma, which only deepened his negative self-perception. He often engaged in a pattern of self-blame, ruminating over what he might have done differently to prevent the violence. Each time he resorted to these maladaptive strategies, it reinforced his belief that he was fragile, unable to cope without hiding his true feelings, adding to his sense of being unworthy of love and safety. These thoughts spiraled into darker places, feeding his belief that he was somehow responsible for the abuse. He would suppress his anger, convinced that expressing it would only lead to further harm, both to himself and to those around him. Each time he engaged in these maladaptive strategies, it reinforced the belief that he was fragile, that he couldn't cope without hiding his true feelings, further entrenching his negative self-image. This emotional suppression manifested in other ways, including a troubling relationship with food; he found himself undereating as a way to cope, convinced that by restricting his intake, he could regain some semblance of control over his life.

As days turned into months, Ethan's sense of safety deteriorated further. He would wake in the middle of the night, gripped by fear, convinced that danger lurked just beyond his door. When he heard the clock tick longer than expected or when a simple delay occurred, his mind would race to dark possibilities, convinced that something bad was about to happen. This heightened sense of threat was compounded by his negative appraisals of the world around him. The constant awareness of potential danger convinced him that he was not the kind of person who deserved safety or peace, further entrenching his negative self-image. Once he had internalized this belief, even minor incidents like a loud noise or a sudden movement would trigger a wave of anxiety, confirming his fears that the world was unsafe and that he was perpetually at risk. Feeling constantly on edge, he had come to accept that this fear was a reflection of his own inadequacy, a belief that he was not the kind of person who deserved to feel safe. This pervasive sense of threat clouded his judgment, making him believe that even the most mundane situations could lead to danger, thus confirming his negative views of himself and the world. The constant sense of danger validated his most fearful thoughts, leading him to conclude that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, which made the world feel even more hostile. He felt a deep-seated conviction that people, in general, could not be trusted, which only fueled his anxiety and avoidance of social interactions. This belief that everyone around him could pose a threat made him hyper-vigilant, believing that he was always in danger, which in turn reinforced his sense of isolation and mistrust. He became increasingly convinced that the world was a dangerous place where harm was always just around the corner.

The memories of the abuse served as a catalyst for his negative beliefs, reinforcing a cycle of self-doubt and mistrust. Every time he recalled the event, the emotional overwhelm would wash over him, leaving him breathless and paralyzed, unable to engage with the reality of his surroundings. After such memories surfaced, he often found himself thinking that if this kept happening, there must be something deeply wrong with him, reinforcing the negative beliefs he had developed about his own worth. These vivid memories led him to internalize a negative self-perception, convincing him that he had somehow let this happen and that it indicated something fundamentally wrong with him. Each time the trauma replayed in his mind, it deepened his belief that he was somehow responsible for the violence, leading him to think of himself as a target rather than a victim. These memories were not distant echoes; they felt immediate and raw, leading him to believe he could never truly escape the impact of the trauma. Each recollection further intensified his belief that he was inadequate, unworthy of love, and unfit to trust anyone.

Now, as Ethan sits in a therapist's office for the first time, he feels a flicker of hope amidst the overwhelming shadows of his past. He is terrified that he will never be able to reclaim his sense of safety or self-worth, yet he longs to break free from the chains of his memories and the fear that has come to dominate his life. He knows he cannot continue to live in isolation, paralyzed by anxiety and mistrust. The journey ahead feels daunting, but the desire to regain control over his life is stronger than the fear that has held him captive for so long.
